name: Churches and Faith Organisations
blurb: Sermon prep, administration, and pastoral limits across hundreds of thousands of congregations, from Barna research and faith-tech platforms to Notre Dame ethics work.

points.desc: Census BTOS covers religious and civic organisations within its service-sector series; no better official measure exists yet, and this page says less rather than guessing.
points.name: Adoption is measured, not guessed

points.name: Barna Group runs the national studies

points.desc: Used by thousands of US churches, Gloo surveys faith leaders and builds AI tooling for ministry - a primary source for what deployment actually looks like in congregations.

points.desc: The interfaith nonprofit network brings scholars, technologists, and clergy together on the ethical deployment of AI in religious contexts.

points.desc: The university's Institute for Ethics and the Common Good funds and tracks research on AI's impact on faith and religious life.
points.name: Notre Dame studies AI and human formation

points.desc: The Hartford Institute for Religion Research regularly surveys congregational trends and digital adoption across American places of worship.
points.name: Hartford surveys congregational technology

points.desc: Pew Research Center's Religion & Public Life work periodically measures how the public and clergy view technology and AI in religious spaces.
points.name: Pew measures public and clergy attitudes

summary: No single body tracks AI adoption across America's hundreds of thousands of congregations - coverage comes from research firms, faith-tech platforms, and academic institutes, and this page names them rather than pretending a census exists. Sermon research, translation, accessibility, and administration are the working uses; every tradition is writing its own guidance.

analysis.body:
# AI Adoption in Churches and Faith Organizations

According to the Census Bureau's Business Time-Use Survey, 12.6% of firms in the religious organizations category (part of NAICS 81, Other Services) reported using AI in the prior two weeks, up from 11.3% in the previous period. This represents the most reliable measure available for the sector, though the category encompasses a broad range of religious and civic organizations rather than congregations alone. The Hartford Institute for Religion Research and Barna Group, which runs national studies on trends affecting faith and ministry, are the primary sources tracking AI adoption more specifically within congregational life, though neither has published granular adoption percentages in the excerpts available here.

The sector's ethical posture distinguishes it from most industries. AI and Faith, an interfaith nonprofit, convenes tech creators, researchers, ethicists, and theologians specifically to inject what it calls "humility and historicity" into AI development and deployment. This framing reflects a broader concern: the organization notes that "emerging issues around control and power, privacy, bias and discrimination, economic well-being, and even our understanding of what it means to be human are all inherent to the ways that AI is created and used in society." For the 85 percent of the world's population claiming religious affiliation, AI and Faith argues these are not only moral but deeply spiritual questions requiring faith-based values and ancient wisdom traditions to shape how the technology is designed and used.

Notre Dame's Institute for Ethics and the Common Good, directed by Meghan Sullivan, advances research specifically on AI and human formation within faith contexts. The institute funds multidisciplinary work examining real-world challenges and developing "practical models and applied solutions for ethical technology design, development, and deployment" in this space. This academic infrastructure reflects growing institutional recognition that deploying AI in congregations raises distinct questions about spiritual formation, pastoral care, and what it means for artificial systems to participate in human and religious life.

On the vendor side, Gloo is the sector's primary technology platform, serving thousands of U.S. churches. Gloo AI delivers what it markets as "values-aligned models, developer tools, and benchmarks for faith-based organizations," claiming the first comprehensive evaluation framework measuring AI alignment across seven research-backed dimensions of human flourishing. Its toolkit includes API-first support for inference, retrieval-augmented generation, and assistant workflows, with infrastructure for knowledge graphs and data integration to enable "ministry insights." Gloo also operates as a marketplace connecting custom-built applications and builder tools across congregations.

The sourced material does not provide specific data on what churches are deploying AI for, return-on-investment evidence, measurable outcomes from deployments, or regulatory guidance specific to faith organizations. Barna Group's reporting on pastoral leadership and the state of congregations, and Pew Research's periodic work on public and clergy attitudes toward technology, are referenced as tracking these trends but their detailed findings on AI use cases and impact are not excerpted here. Faith leaders considering AI deployment should weigh the sector's strong emphasis on ethical alignment and human flourishing against the relative absence of published data on practical ROI or long-term effects on congregational life.
